General provisions and rules common to the weapon categories

Introduction

GEN-1.1

The aim of the event is to evaluate fencing in a safe and friendly manner, according to the principle “hit without being hit”. Similarly to historical rulesets, the competition tests deliberately abstracted skills; it is not a simulation of an unrestricted fight continued to the bitter end. In this sense, every point is treated as a separate “duel” within the framework of the rules below; losing such a duel is indicated by a point awarded against the losing fencer. Our goal is to establish a relative ranking and identify, over the competition day(s), the fencer who proves best in tactical, technical and athletic ability.

GEN-1.2

A fundamental principle above all others is sportsmanship. Any workable ruleset must be effective in ensuring equal opportunity for all participants.

Scope of the rules

Explanation of the technical terms most commonly used in refereeing

Explanation of the technical terms most commonly used in judging fencing actions.

Preamble

It is emphasised that this section does not replace fencing treatises; it is included to help the reader understand the rules.

Fencing time

Fencing time is the time required to perform one simple fencing action.

Offensive and defensive actions

Definitions

GEN-3.2.1

Offensive actions (attack, riposte, counter-riposte).

GEN-3.2.1.1

Attack — the initial offensive action, made by extending the arm and continuously threatening the opponent’s valid target, preceding the initiation of the lunge, flèche, or other weapon-specific offensive footwork.

GEN-3.2.1.2

Riposte — the offensive action made by the fencer who has parried the attack.

GEN-3.2.1.3

Counter-riposte — the offensive action made by the fencer who has parried the riposte.

GEN-3.2.2

Defensive actions are called parries.

  • A parry is a defensive action made with the weapon to prevent an offensive action from arriving.

Explanations

Offensive actions

GEN-3.2.3

Attack

GEN-3.2.3.1

An action is simple when it is executed in one movement:

  • either direct (in the same line),
  • or indirect (in another line).

GEN-3.2.3.2

An action is compound when it is executed in several movements.

GEN-3.2.4

Riposte (thrust/cut back)
A riposte may be immediate or delayed, depending on the nature and speed of the action. The riposte may be:

GEN-3.2.4.1

  • Simple, direct
  • Direct riposte: hits without leaving the line in which the parry was made.
  • Riposte along the blade: hits by grazing along the blade after the parry.

GEN-3.2.4.2

Simple, indirect

  • Riposte by disengagement: hits in the opposite line to that in which the parry was formed.
  • Riposte with a coupé: hits in the opposite line to that in which the parry was formed, the blade passing over the opponent’s point.

GEN-3.2.4.3

Compound riposte

  • Riposte with a doublé: hits in the opposite line after describing a full circle around the opponent’s blade.
  • Riposte with a one–two: hits in the same line after first having gone into the opposite line by passing under the opponent’s blade.

GEN-3.2.5

Counter-attacks

Counter-attacks are offensive or offensive–defensive actions made during the opponent’s offensive action.

GEN-3.2.5.1

Stop hit: a counter-attack made into an attack.

GEN-3.2.5.2

Stop hit with opposition: a stop hit made while closing the line in which the opponent’s attack will be completed.

GEN-3.2.5.3

Stop hit made within a period of fencing time (“in time”): a stop hit made at the moment of the attacker’s hesitation, feint, or badly executed attack. In Longsword-VOR, a started attack has priority; a stop hit is considered successful only if clearly “in tempo” (it lands before the final movement of the attack begins) or the attacker does not hit at all.

GEN-3.2.6

Other offensive actions — a further offensive action after the initial attack.

GEN-3.2.6.1

Remise: a simple immediate offensive action, following the original attack without withdrawing the arm, after the opponent has parried or retreated, when the opponent either breaks blade contact without riposting or makes a delayed/indirect riposte, or makes a compound riposte.

GEN-3.2.6.2

Redoublement: a new simple or compound action against an opponent who has parried without riposting, or who avoided the first action merely by retreating or displacing the target.

GEN-3.2.6.3

Reprise of the attack: a new attack executed immediately after a return to the on-guard position.

GEN-3.2.6.4

Counter-time: any action made by the attacker against a stop hit made by the opponent.

Defensive actions

GEN-3.2.7

Parry

  • A parry is simple, direct when it is made in the same line as the attack.
  • A circular parry is made in the opposite line to that of the attack.

“Point in line” position

GEN-3.2.8

The point in line position is a specific position in which the fencer’s arm is kept extended and the point of the weapon continually threatens the opponent’s valid target.

The field of play

GEN-4.1

The surface of the field of play is even and horizontal. It must not provide advantage or disadvantage to either fencer, especially with respect to lighting.

GEN-4.2

That portion of the field of play which is used for fencing is called the piste.

GEN-4.3

The piste/arena is square or rectangular. The minimum permitted bounding size is 6×9 metres and the maximum is 8×12 metres. The boundaries must be marked along their full length in a way that adheres well to the floor. The nearest obstacle must be at least 1 metre from the boundary.

GEN-4.4

The starting positions of the fencers must be clearly marked on the floor such that they are at least 2 metres from the centre, leaving at least 4 metres between the two fencers at the start of the bout.

Equipment

Compliance

GEN-5.1.1

Fencers arm, equip and clothe themselves and fence at their own responsibility and at their own risk.

GEN-5.1.2

At the venue of official MHS competitions (including training halls linked to the competition), any fencer who warms up or trains must wear fencing clothing and equipment complying with MHS requirements. Any person giving a lesson must wear at least an MHS-compliant master’s plastron, glove and mask. Any fencer taking a lesson must wear at least a mask and a glove. The MHS Supervisor of the competition or a member of the Organising Team penalises any person not respecting this rule with a yellow card, followed by a black card in case of repeated infringement.

GEN-5.1.3

The safety measures specified in this ruleset and the attached standards are designed to reinforce safety but cannot guarantee it. Responsibility cannot be transferred to MHS, organisers, officials, or any person who may cause an accident.

For steel weapons

GEN-5.2.1

Head protection

GEN-5.2.1.1

An undamaged FIE-approved mask (CE level 2, 1600N resistance) is mandatory.

GEN-5.2.1.2

A HEMA-specific back-of-head and cervical spine protector compatible with the mask is mandatory.

GEN-5.2.1.3

A rigid or semi-rigid thick throat protector is mandatory.

GEN-5.2.1.4

The bib of the mask must not fold up.

GEN-5.2.1.5

When wearing complete head protection (mask + back-of-head protector + throat protector), turning the head in any usual direction must not expose uncovered skin on the head/neck.

GEN-5.2.2

Hand, arm and torso protection

GEN-5.2.2.1

Only gloves designed specifically for HEMA competition (e.g. Sparring Gloves) or gloves meeting all special requirements may be used. Gloves containing any metal components are forbidden (except minor reinforcement fittings such as eyelets for elastic straps).

GEN-5.2.2.2

Competition gloves are not required to have a reinforced palm layer, but the full palm must be covered; a simple textile glove layer is sufficient for palm coverage.

GEN-5.2.2.3

The upper body must be protected by an undamaged fencing jacket or gambeson made of a material that prevents blade penetration and cushions impact or thrust. The jacket is inspected by equipment check staff and the Referee. It must cover the armpit area and have at least 350N puncture resistance. The collar must be designed to catch upward-sliding blades; using folded puncture-resistant material is recommended.

GEN-5.2.2.4

All competitors must wear rigid chest protection.

GEN-5.2.2.5

If the jacket alone does not sufficiently protect the elbow and forearm, additional rigid protection is mandatory.

GEN-5.2.2.6

The whole body surface must be covered by appropriate protective clothing. No bare skin may remain between glove and jacket.

GEN-5.2.2.7

An 800N (FIE, single-sided) underarm protector is recommended; mandatory introduction is planned.

GEN-5.2.3

Leg protection

GEN-5.2.3.1

Groin protection is mandatory for all male and female competitors.

GEN-5.2.3.2

Knees and shins must be protected from front and sides with rigid protection.

GEN-5.2.3.3

Hips must be protected by the jacket, separate hip protection (e.g. padded skirt) or padded trousers.

GEN-5.2.3.4

Thighs, groin and hips must be covered by trousers rated at least CE Level 1 (350N) or other approved puncture-resistant material.

GEN-5.2.3.5

Between jacket and trousers there must be no body surface lacking adequate protection. Waist-high fencing trousers are recommended.

GEN-5.2.4

Weapons

Each fencer is responsible for their own weapon. The weapon must be presented in proper condition at the competition: free of burrs and rust, and with any previous tip tape removed. Weapons are inspected by designated staff per the requirements below; if compliant, staff will tape the tip with a visible tape. The piste Referee may re-check weapons at any time and may ban weapons with significant damage. After a weapon is banned, the Referee may allow up to 5 minutes for replacement. If the fencer cannot comply within the time limit, they may not continue and may be excluded from the event.

GEN-5.2.5

Longsword

GEN-5.2.5.1

Only straight-bladed European-type fencing/training swords are permitted. A longsword must have a double-edged blade, a crossguard and a pommel. It must be made of suitable steel (wood, aluminium and plastic swords are forbidden) and must meet the following:

GEN-5.2.5.2

Severely damaged blades are forbidden; blades may not be bent, broken, burred or rusty. Edges must be blunt and rounded.

GEN-5.2.5.3

The base of the blade may flare, but all edges and projections must be rounded and blunt.

GEN-5.2.5.4

The crossguard must be straight with rounded ends. Additional protection (e.g. rings) is not permitted.

GEN-5.2.5.5

The pommel must have a smooth surface and must not have sharp rivets or spikes.

GEN-5.2.5.6

Blade flexibility is tested by a bend test against a scale; the maximum kilogram value indicated by the scale represents flexibility. Longsword flexibility must be between 9–16 kg.

GEN-5.2.5.7

The tip must be at least 1 cm wide.

GEN-5.2.5.8

The tip must be blunt, rounded, and either flared or bent back in an arc to reduce the risk of piercing.

GEN-5.2.5.9

The point of balance must not be more than 9 cm beyond the blade-side edge of the crossguard.

GEN-5.2.5.10

The tip must be taped on-site with a coloured, clearly visible tape for better visibility.

GEN-5.2.5.11

Overall length must be 120–140 cm.

GEN-5.2.5.12

Total mass (men’s event): 1300–1800 g.

GEN-5.2.5.13

Total mass (women’s event): 1100–1600 g.

GEN-5.2.6

Rapier

Under development.

GEN-5.2.7

Sword and buckler

Under development.

GEN-5.3

For padded weapons

GEN-5.3.1

Protective equipment

GEN-5.3.1.1

An undamaged mask (minimum CE level 1, 350N resistance) is mandatory.

GEN-5.3.1.2

A rigid or semi-rigid thick throat protector is mandatory.

GEN-5.3.1.3

The mask bib must not fold up.

GEN-5.3.1.4

Rigid chest protection is mandatory for all women. For men it is not mandatory but strongly recommended.

GEN-5.3.1.5

At least hockey/lacrosse/Red Dragon type padded gloves (or similar) must be worn.

GEN-5.3.2

Padded weapons

GEN-5.3.2.1

Undamaged.

GEN-5.3.2.2

Weight …–… g (under development).

GEN-5.3.2.3

Overall length must be 120–140 cm.

GEN-5.3.2.4

No sharp or injurious parts are permitted.

GEN-5.3.2.5

Weapons with metal fittings are forbidden.

Fencing

Coming on guard and the position of the fencers

GEN-6.1.1

The fencer whose name is called first must stand on the Referee’s right, except in a bout between a right- and a left-hander where the left-hander is called first.

GEN-6.1.2

The team with more right-handed fencers stands on the Referee’s right. If equal numbers, the team called first stands on the Referee’s right.

GEN-6.1.3

The Referee places the competitors facing each other so that their front foot is directly behind the on-guard line.

GEN-6.1.4

At the beginning of the bout and thereafter, the fencers are always placed in the centre line of the piste.

GEN-6.1.5

When placed on guard during the bout, the distance between the fencers must be such that, in the point-in-line position with arm extended, the points cannot touch.

GEN-6.1.6

After a valid hit, the fencers are placed on guard in the middle of the piste.

GEN-6.1.7

If no hit is awarded, they are replaced where they were when the fight was interrupted. Returning to correct distance must not force a fencer who was inside the rear boundary at the moment of interruption to step back beyond it. If they already had one foot behind the rear line, they remain there.

GEN-6.1.8

(In direct elimination bouts) at the beginning of each period and any additional 1-minute extension, the fencers are placed on guard in the middle of the piste.

GEN-6.1.9

The fencers come on guard at the Referee’s command “On guard!”. The Referee then asks “Ready?”; on an affirmative reply or in absence of a negative reply, the Referee starts the bout with “Play!”.

GEN-6.1.10

Until “Play!”, fencers must remain correctly on guard and completely still.

GEN-6.1.11

When applying VOR rules/weapon variant, coming on guard may not be done in the point-in-line position.

Beginning, stopping and restarting the bout

GEN-6.2.1

Before the start of the bout, the Referee asks the opponents to agree whether grappling holds are allowed during body-to-body fighting in their bout. This must be noted on the score sheet.

GEN-6.2.2

The start of the bout is signalled by “Play!”. Any movement executed or initiated before the command is not counted.

GEN-6.2.3

The bout stops on the command “Halt!”, except in special situations which modify the regular and normal conditions of the bout (see GEN-6.10.9, GEN-6.10.9 as well): GEN-6.2.4, GEN-6.2.5, GEN-6.2.6, GEN-6.2.7.

GEN-6.2.4

After “Halt!”, a fencer may not start a new action; only a movement begun before the order remains valid. Everything which occurs afterwards is not valid (but see GEN-6.10.9, GEN-6.10.9).

GEN-6.2.5

If a fencer stops before “Halt!” and is hit, the hit is valid.

GEN-6.2.6

“Halt!” must also be called if the fencing becomes dangerous, confused or contrary to the rules; if a fencer becomes disarmed (except in wrestling contexts); or if a fencer leaves the piste/arena.

GEN-6.2.7

Except in exceptional circumstances, the Referee may not allow a fencer to leave the piste. If a fencer leaves without permission, first-group penalties apply.

GEN-6.2.8

Fencers may request the bout to be stopped by raising their hand, for any valid reason (e.g. equipment failure, injury). The bout is considered stopped only when the Referee gives the command “Halt!”.

GEN-6.2.9

Actions initiated before the start command or after the stop command are not valid. Initiating an action before “Play!” or after “Halt!” is a first-group disciplinary offence.

GEN-6.2.10

The Referee may disregard non-valid hits if they can clearly follow subsequent actions.

GEN-6.2.11

If the Referee stops the bout because they believed an earlier hit was invalid and ignored it, but it later becomes clear the earlier hit was valid, the Referee must, if possible, decide taking the first valid hit into account, even if this requires annulling later hits.

GEN-6.2.12

At the end of the pools and every direct elimination bout, before leaving the field of play, fencers check and sign the score sheet kept by the Referee or staff. In team matches this is done by the team captains.

GEN-6.2.13

In case of equipment failure during the bout, the Referee may allow a break of up to 5 minutes (starting when the Referee confirms the failure). This time may be used for repair or replacement and re-checking. If the competitor cannot continue by the end of the break, the Referee may exclude the competitor from that bout. See ORG-2.3.13.

Close quarters

GEN-6.3.1

Fencing at close quarters is permitted so long as the competitors can wield their weapons correctly and the Referee can follow the action.

Body contact

GEN-6.4.1

It is forbidden intentionally to cause body contact to avoid being hit or to push the opponent, except where the fighters have approved the use of gripping and wrestling actions before the bout. In case of such an offence, first-group penalties apply and any hit scored by the fencer at fault is annulled.

GEN-6.4.2

A fencer does not transgress the basic conventions and is not penalised if, by a flèche attack or vigorous advance, they cause body contact even repeatedly, without brutality or violence.

Body contact and flèche

GEN-6.5.1

A flèche systematically ending in body contact (as referenced here) must not be confused with a flèche resulting in a shock that jostles the opponent; the latter is intentional brutality and is punished as a second-group offence at all weapons.

GEN-6.5.2

Conversely, a running flèche (even passing the opponent) without body contact is not forbidden. The Referee must not call “Halt!” too soon so as not to annul a possible riposte. In a running flèche that does not hit the opponent, if the fencer crosses the boundary, they are considered hit (see: leaving the arena).

Displacing the target and passing

GEN-6.6.1

Displacement and ducking are allowed, including where the unarmed hand and/or the knee of the rear leg contacts the floor.

GEN-6.6.2

Turning one’s back on the opponent during the bout is forbidden. First-group penalties apply and any hit scored by the fencer at fault is annulled.

Substituting valid target surfaces

GEN-6.7.1

If a fencer covers or moves a valid target surface by blocking or irregular movement, the fencer is penalised by the Referee with first-group penalties as listed in DIS-4.1.1–DIS-4.1.5, DIS-4.1.9, DIS-4.3.20, and any hit scored by the fencer at fault is annulled.

Grappling and wrestling actions

GEN-6.8.1

Gripping and wrestling (grabbing/control/throw/takedown) are permitted within a bout only if both parties consent before the bout starts. If one party does not accept wrestling, no explanation is required. In team matches, each team member decides individually whether they accept wrestling with the given opponent.

GEN-6.8.2

A wrestling action includes any close-quarter action not executed with the weapon (hand/foot/head techniques, holds, disarms, strikes), as well as weapon actions which, instead of direct hitting, aim to manipulate the opponent's body parts. If either opponent did not consent to wrestling, initiating any wrestling action is a first-group offence.

GEN-6.8.3 The Referee may stop the bout after prolonged unsuccessful close quarters or wrestling (at the Referee’s discretion). Grabbing an opponent’s momentarily neutralised blade is permitted. A point may be awarded only if the blade grab is brief and is immediately followed by a weapon hit. If no hit results from the grab, the Referee stops without awarding a point. If the initiating party does not neutralise the opponent’s weapon first and receives a hit, the point is awarded against the initiator.

GEN-6.8.4

Scoring wrestling actions:

GEN-6.8.4.1

With a wrestling hold, lifting at least one of the opponent’s feet off the ground. (Throws/takedowns must NOT be completed.)

GEN-6.8.4.2

Wrestling holds with or without the weapon that prevent the opponent's movement/escape. The Referee judges whether the control position exists and is valid; once the Referee judges the control/dominance requirements are met, they call "Halt!" and award 1 point against the dominated fencer.

GEN-6.8.4.3 A dominance/control judgement is not applicable in positions where the opponent can break out and initiate valid actions, even if, by active effort, the dominating weapon continues to touch the opponent’s target. The Referee judges validity at their discretion.

GEN-6.8.5

After a takedown, further fighting is not permitted. The Referee calls "Halt!" if either fencer goes to the ground, or if the Referee cannot judge the action, or if dominance cannot be obtained over a prolonged period (Referee's discretion).

GEN-6.8.6

A disarm (where one fencer, by intentional close-quarter action, takes the opponent's weapon) is a valid scoring method, except if the disarmed fencer immediately (before "Halt!") controls the opponent's blade and continues wrestling.

GEN-6.8.7 If a fencer drops their weapon or falls without opponent intervention, the Referee calls “Halt!”. A hit achieved by a movement that began before the opponent clearly lost their weapon or fell must be considered valid even if it lands afterwards. By sportsmanship, it is improper to initiate a new attack against an opponent who has lost their weapon or fallen; therefore no point is awarded for such a new attack.

Ground gained or lost

GEN-6.9.1

When "Halt!" is called, ground gained is held until a hit is awarded. If no hit is awarded, on re-placing on guard both fencers should retire an equal distance to keep fencing distance.

GEN-6.9.2

However, if the bout was stopped because of body contact (and close quarters is not allowed), the fencers are placed on guard so that the fencer who sustained the body contact remains where they were; this also applies if the opponent made a flèche attack even without body contact.

Crossing the boundaries

GEN-6.9.1

If a competitor crosses completely (with both feet) any boundary line of the arena, the Referee must immediately call “Halt!” and must annul everything that occurred after the boundary was crossed.

GEN-6.9.2

However, a hit by a fencer who steps out with only one foot remains valid if the action began before “Halt!”, even if the fencer subsequently completely leaves the arena.

GEN-6.9.3

If a fencer leaves the piste completely (both feet), only a hit made by the fencer who remains at least one foot inside may be awarded, and only in Longsword-Combat and Longsword-Afterblow (even in case of simultaneous hits). In Longsword-VOR, the convention rules apply.

GEN-6.9.4

If a fencer steps completely beyond a boundary (both feet) without having scored a valid hit before exiting:

  • on the first exit, the fencer receives a warning;
  • on any further exit in the same bout, the exiting competitor is penalised by a hit against them (the opponent receives one point), even if the competitor was not actually hit.

GEN-6.9.5

Accidental stepping out: no penalty applies where a fencer leaves the boundary not intentionally but due to unexpected events/accidents (e.g. being pushed).

Duration of the bout

GEN-6.11.1

The duration of a bout means effective fighting time, i.e. the total of time intervals between "Play!" and "Halt!".

GEN-6.11.2

Time is controlled by the Referee or a timekeeper. In bouts where the timer is visible to spectators (strongly recommended for finals), the timer must be placed so it is visible to both fencers and the Referee.

GEN-6.11.3

A finished bout or relay segment may not be restarted, even if there was a formal error.

Framework for individual pool bouts

GEN-6.11.4 In individual pool bouts, a bout ends when any of the following conditions is met:

GEN-6.10.4.1

One fencer reaches the defined number of hits (or in Afterblow: the defined score):

GEN-6.10.4.1.1

VOR: one fencer reaches 5 hits.

GEN-6.10.4.1.2

Combat:

  • one fencer reaches 5 hits, or
  • if the score reaches 4–4, a decisive hit must be scored before the time limit ends. Double hits are not taken into account (and the fencers remain where they were on the piste).

GEN-6.10.4.1.3

Afterblow:

  • one fencer reaches at least 7 POINTS,
    • due to weighting, the score may exceed 7;
    • if both fencers reach or exceed 7 points at the same time (simultaneous hits):
      • if the point difference is at least 1, the bout ends;
      • if the score is tied, the scores must be reset to 6–6 and a decisive hit must be scored before the time limit ends. Equivalent simultaneous hits are not taken into account (and the fencers remain where they were on the piste).

GEN-6.10.4.1.4

The score sheet records the final score (VN–Dn, where N = winner’s points and n = loser’s points).

GEN-6.10.4.5

Or three minutes of effective fighting time elapses:

GEN-6.10.4.5.1

If, when time expires, there is at least a one-hit difference between the fencers’ scores, the fencer with the higher score is declared the winner. The score sheet records the hits/points actually scored in the bout (VN–Dn, where N = winner’s points and n = loser’s points).

GEN-6.10.4.5.2

If, when time expires, the score is tied, the fencers fence for a decisive hit for up to one minute. Before restarting fencing, the Referee draws lots to decide who will be the winner if the score remains tied after the one minute.

GEN-6.10.4.5.3

In this case, the score sheet records the hits/points actually scored during the bout as follows:

  • VN–Dn, if a decisive hit was scored within the time limit;
  • V6–D6, or V4–D4, or V2–D2, or V1–D1, or V0–D0, if the winner is determined by drawing lots.

Framework for individual direct elimination bouts

GEN-6.10.5

An individual direct elimination bout ends when any of the following conditions is met:

GEN-6.10.5.1

One fencer reaches the defined number of hits (or in Afterblow: the defined score):

GEN-6.10.5.1.1

VOR: one fencer reaches 10 hits.

GEN-6.10.5.1.2

Combat:

  • one fencer reaches 10 hits;
  • if both fencers reach 10 points at the same time (simultaneous hits), they must score a decisive hit before the time limit ends. Equivalent simultaneous hits are not taken into account (and the fencers remain where they were on the piste).

GEN-6.10.5.1.3

Afterblow:

  • one fencer reaches at least 11 POINTS;
    • due to weighting, the score may exceed 11;
    • if both fencers reach or exceed 11 points at the same time (simultaneous hits):
      • if the point difference is at least 1, the bout ends;
      • if the score is tied, they must score a decisive hit before the time limit ends. Equivalent simultaneous hits are not taken into account (and the fencers remain where they were on the piste).

GEN-6.10.5.2

Or the defined effective fencing time elapses: Two three-minute periods (6 minutes of effective fencing time) separated by two one-minute rest breaks.

GEN-6.10.5.2.1

In VOR, the first period lasts either until three minutes elapse or until one of the fencers reaches 5 hits.

GEN-6.10.5.2.2

If, when the time defined by the rules expires, the scores are tied, the fencers fence for a winning hit for up to one minute. Before restarting fencing, the Referee draws lots (coin toss) to decide who will be the winner if the scores remain tied after the additional minute.

GEN-6.10.5.3

During the one-minute rest break, one person designated before the bout may approach the competitor closely.

GEN-6.10.5.4

The points recorded on the score sheet are the points actually scored during the bout.

GEN-6.10.6

Team matches

GEN-6.10.6.1

Each relay in the team match is fenced to 5 hits (5, 10, 15, 20, etc.). Exceptionally, a relay may end with more than 5, 10, 15, etc. if a fencer scores a valid hit at the end of the relay and an additional penalty hit is also awarded; in this case both are counted. The maximum time for each relay is 2 minutes.

GEN-6.10.6.2

The first two opponents fence until one reaches 5 hits within the 2-minute time limit. The next two competitors then fence within the 2-minute time limit until one reaches 10 hits, and so on, adding five hits to the target score for each subsequent relay.

GEN-6.10.6.3

If, after two minutes, the target score for the relay has not been reached, the next two competitors continue the match from the score at which it was stopped, and fence within the 2-minute time limit up to the maximum score prescribed for that relay.

GEN-6.10.6.4

The winning team is the team that reaches the maximum of 45 hits, or the team that has scored more hits when time expires.

GEN-6.10.6.5

If, when the time for the last relay expires, the score is tied, the competitors fencing the last relay fence for a decisive hit for up to one minute. Before restarting fencing, the Referee draws lots to decide who will be the winner if the score remains tied after the one minute.

Timekeeping

Interruption of the fight

GEN-6.10.7
Each time the fight is interrupted, the fencers may ask how much time remains.

GEN-6.10.8

A fencer who attempts to interrupt the bout without justification or to prolong interruptions is penalised as a first-group offence.

GEN-6.10.9

After the regulated time has expired, the timekeeper must call “Halt!” (or operate an audible signal) to stop the fight, and a hit initiated but landing after time has expired is not valid.

GEN-6.10.10

If no visible timer is provided for the fencers, the timekeeper must give a “One minute!” warning (or audible signal) 60 seconds before the end — without stopping the fight.

GEN-6.10.11

The Referee remains responsible for timekeeping throughout the bout. In case of timekeeping device failure, the Referee determines the remaining fencing time.

Injury or other medical reasons; withdrawal

GEN-6.11.1

If during the bout an injury or other medical issue arises and is certified by the on-duty doctor and/or medical provider, the Referee may allow a break of up to 5 minutes. The break is reserved exclusively for treatment. If the doctor determines the fencer cannot continue, the doctor may decide the fencer must retire (individual) or be replaced if possible (team). All such breaks must be recorded.

GEN-6.11.2

On the same day, a further break may be granted only for a different injury/medical incident.

GEN-6.11.3

If a fencer requests a break that the doctor deems unjustified, the Referee penalises the fencer as a second-group offence.

GEN-6.11.4

In team events, a fencer deemed unable to continue a bout may nevertheless fence in subsequent team matches the same day based on the doctor’s opinion.

GEN-6.11.5

For efficient running of the competition, the organiser may change bout order in pools.

Forbidden actions

GEN-6.11.1

Neck cranks, lifting the opponent, full joint locks, small joint locks, large-arc throws and other potentially dangerous wrestling techniques; strikes (including headbutts, knees, elbows); kicks; violent pushes; and throwing the weapon are strictly forbidden.

GEN-6.11.2

Excessive force, brutality and unnecessary violence are forbidden.

GEN-6.11.3

It is forbidden to strike the back of the head, the spine, the back of the knee, and the foot.

GEN-6.11.4

Hitting the floor due to misjudging distance or movement is a first-group offence (the Referee may ignore light floor contacts that occur after hitting the opponent, as a consequence of the opponent’s action, or accidentally).

GEN-6.11.5

Hitting with the crossguard is forbidden.

Conduct of the bout and judging hits

The Referee

GEN-7.1.1.1

By accepting appointment as referee or assistant referee, the person so appointed pledges on their honour to respect the rules and to carry out their duties with strict impartiality and full attention.

GEN-7.1.1.2

Referees may not simultaneously hold any other role at the competition (e.g. Organising Team member, team captain, official delegate of their federation, coach, etc.).

GEN-7.1.2

The Referee’s duties include calling and checking in the fencers; directing the bout; checking weapons/clothing/equipment; directing assistants; positioning to follow the bout; penalising offences; awarding hits; maintaining order; and ensuring the arena is safe.

GEN-7.1.3

After stopping the bout, the Referee consults with the assistant referee if needed, verbally and/or by signals.

Assistant referee

GEN-7.2.1

The Referee is assisted by an assistant referee in judging points and evaluating hits.

GEN-7.2.2

The main task of the assistant referee is to observe the bout from an angle different from the Referee’s (from the other side of the fencers). After the Referee stops the bout, the assistant referee contributes to judging the action if needed.

GEN-7.2.3

The assistant referee is not responsible for awarding points nor for the final outcome of the bout.

Video referees

GEN-7.3.1

When video refereeing is used, designated video consultants watch the bout live and, if necessary, on screen, and consult with the Referee.

Assignment of referees and video referees

Judging hits

GEN-7.5.1

The materiality of the hit is established by the Referee, consulting the assistant referee if needed.

GEN-7.5.2

The Referee disregards hits which are made before “Play!” or after “Halt!”, or which are made on objects other than the opponent or equipment.

GEN-7.5.3

A hit made during or after a fall must be annulled.

GEN-7.5.4

A competitor who deliberately drops their weapon during the fencing phrase is penalised as a second-group offence. However, a hit scored by the opponent remains valid provided the action began before “Halt!”.

GEN-7.5.5

In accordance with the general rules, the Referee must stop the bout if the fencing becomes confused and the Referee can no longer follow its course, even if no hit was scored.

Validity or priority of the hit

GEN-7.5.6

When stopping the fight, the Referee briefly analyses the actions which make up the last fencing phrase.

GEN-7.5.4

After deciding on the materiality of the hit, the Referee, by applying the rules, determines which fencer a hit must be awarded against (possibly against both), or that no valid hit was scored.

Possibility of video review

GEN-7.5.6

Requesting video review: in both team and individual competitions, only the fencer currently on the piste is entitled to request video review.

GEN-7.5.7

In individual competition, the fencer on the piste may request video review:

  • once per bout in pool bouts;
  • twice per bout in direct elimination bouts.

GEN-7.5.8

If the Referee agrees with the competitor requesting the replay, the competitor’s right to request video review is not lost.

GEN-7.5.9

In team competitions, competitors have the right to request video review once per relay. If the Referee agrees with the competitor’s request, this right remains available.

GEN-7.5.10

If video review is requested, the Referee walks to the video referee; together they review the video and, after analysing the action, the Referee communicates the final decision.

GEN-7.5.11

At the Referee’s discretion, the review is viewed in real time or in slow motion, at a speed chosen by the Referee.

GEN-7.5.12

At any weapon, the Referee may at any time decide to consult the screen before making a decision.

GEN-7.5.13

At the end of the bout, if the score is tied, the Referee must use video refereeing before awarding the decisive hit.

GEN-7.5.14

The video referee may at any time request the Referee to apply video refereeing.

GEN-7.5.15

Once the Referee has analysed the action together with the video referee — regardless of whether it was initiated by the Referee, requested by the fencer, required due to a tie before the decisive hit, or requested by the video referee — the Referee’s decision is final, and no further review of the same action may be requested.

Referee hand signals

GEN-7.5.16

The Referee must use the following signals:

Regulation equipment and equipment checks by the Referee

GEN-7.6.1

Before each round the Referee checks the required standard markings and equipment-check markings, and that competitors appear with complete equipment and clothing.

GEN-7.6.2

Before the start of each pool bout, team match or direct elimination bout, the Referee calls the fencers together to check the following:

  • for all weapons, that the fencers’ equipment bears the required 350N marking (clothing, mask);
  • that everyone wears a regulation fencing jacket;
  • for all weapons, that everyone has a regulation 800N underarm protector worn under the clothing (currently not mandatory, but strongly recommended until a rules change, and must be checked);
  • that the weapons bear a weapon control mark;
  • for all weapons, that fencers do not carry any electronic communication device that would allow a person outside the piste to communicate with a fencer during the bout.

GEN-7.6.3

In pool bouts, the Referee’s weapon check is carried out when calling the fencers to assemble.

GEN-7.6.4

In direct elimination bouts and finals, the Referee’s weapon check is carried out in the assembly area.

GEN-7.6.5

In addition to the above checks, the Referee leading the bout may at any time carry out checks on their own initiative, or at the request of the fencer or team captain; the Referee may also verify previously performed certification or order additional checks.

GEN-7.6.6

Checked spare equipment is placed by the Referee at the start of the bout next to the piste, on the appropriate fencer’s side.

Non-regulation equipment

GEN-7.7.1

In any situation, if a competitor is found (within the meaning of the Equipment Rules) to possess non-regulation or defective equipment, the Referee confiscates it and submits it to an on-duty expert for examination. The owner may receive the equipment back only after the necessary checks have been completed and any costs arising from repairing the defect have been reimbursed. Before being put back into use, the equipment must be checked again.

GEN-7.7.2

If a fencer appears on the piste:

  • with a defective or non-regulation weapon, or
  • in non-regulation clothing, the Referee applies the penalty corresponding to first-group offences.

GEN-7.7.3

If during the bout an irregularity in the equipment is identified which may have arisen as a consequence of the fight (for example: a hole in the clothing; rigid protective equipment or glove breaks or falls apart; mask is deformed; the weapon fails), then the Referee applies neither warning nor penalty, and awards any regulation hit scored with the failed equipment.

GEN-7.7.4

If, when reporting on the piste or during the bout, it is established that the fencer’s equipment:

GEN-7.7.4.1

lacks a certification/control mark. In this case, the Referee:

  • annuls the last hit (if any) scored by the fencer at fault;
  • applies the penalty corresponding to second-group offences.

GEN-7.7.4.2

is defective in a part that was not checked during pre-competition certification. In this case, the Referee applies the penalty corresponding to second-group offences.

GEN-7.7.4.3

passed pre-competition certification but is suitable for cheating.

GEN-7.7.4.4

bears a certification mark, but the mark is forged or transferred from elsewhere.

GEN-7.7.4.5

has been intentionally modified (i.e. not by accident or due to circumstances during the bout) in a way that it would not pass pre-competition certification.

GEN-7.7.4.7

contains equipment enabling electronic communication, making it possible for a fencer to communicate with a person outside the piste.

GEN-7.7.4.8

  • In the cases GEN-7.7.4.3, GEN-7.7.4.4, GEN-7.7.4.5, and GEN-7.7.4.7, the Referee immediately confiscates the equipment (weapon and, as needed, jacket, mask, underarm protector, trousers, etc.) and hands it to the on-duty expert.

  • After obtaining the expert’s fact-finding opinion, without applying the disadvantages described in DIS-2.1.4/DIS-2.1.6:

    • in the cases GEN-7.7.4.3, GEN-7.7.4.4, GEN-7.7.4.5, and GEN-7.7.4.7, the Referee applies the sanction corresponding to fourth-group offences.

GEN-7.7.4.7

Until the Referee’s decision, the given bout is suspended; however, other bouts of the pool may continue.

Longsword

General rules for longsword fencing

Method of scoring a hit

LS-1.1.1

The longsword is a thrusting and cutting weapon.

LS-1.1.2

Any cut delivered with the flat, the long or the short edge of the blade, as well as any thrust, is acceptable provided it is executed in such a way that—assuming a sharp weapon—it would cause injury to an unarmoured opponent. A hit with the flat may be considered valid if it is the result of a coordinated and effective action.

LS-1.1.3

Cuts delivered “through the blade” which simultaneously contact the opponent’s valid target area and the opponent’s weapon are valid when they land cleanly on the valid target area.

LS-1.1.3

Pommel hits are valid if they strike the uncovered part of the mask grille in a clearly demonstrative way (including with the pommel covered by the glove) and are executed safely. Pommel actions delivered with unnecessary force must be penalised under the second group of offences.

LS-1.1.4

In all three weapon categories, defensive actions may only be executed with the weapon, except where the fighters have explicitly allowed gripping and wrestling actions (see: close-quarter and wrestling rules).

LS-1.1.5

The weapon may not be used—permanently or temporarily, openly or disguised—as a throwing weapon. The weapon must be handled such that at least one hand remains on the grip at all times.

Valid target

LS-1.2.1

Only hits that land on the valid target area are valid.

LS-1.2.2

The valid target area includes the fencer’s entire body, including the weapon’s grip, clothing and protective equipment, except the back of the head, the spine, the feet and the back of the knees.

LS-1.2.3

It is forbidden to protect the valid target or to substitute another body part for it by covering/substitution; any hit scored by the fencer at fault must be annulled.

LS-1.2.3.1

If during the fencing phrase a fencer covers or substitutes their valid target, they must be penalised under the first group of offences.

LS-1.2.3.2

If during the fencing phrase a properly delivered hit is registered as off-target due to covering/substitution, the fencer at fault must be penalised under the first group of offences and the hit must be awarded.

LS-1.2.3

If a hit lands outside the valid target area, it does not count as a hit; it does not stop the fencing phrase and it does not annul subsequent hits. However, a hit delivered after a fencing fault does not count as a valid hit, but it stops the fencing phrase and annuls all hits that follow it.

LS-1.2.4

Judging the force of cuts and thrusts that land on non-valid target areas, and imposing any necessary penalties, is the Referee’s responsibility.

LS-1.2.5

The Referee must penalise any fencer who substitutes a non-valid target area for a valid one—either by covering or by abnormal movement—according to the first group of disciplinary offences.

Establishing or annulling hits

LS-1.3.1

The basis for judging hits is the observations of the Referee who is watching the action, and their assistant.

LS-1.3.2

Only the Referee has authority to judge the validity of a hit according to the weapon rules. The Referee’s findings of fact concerning events they observed are not subject to challenge.

LS-1.3.3

A fencer may, in accordance with the rules, request an explanation, video review, and as a last resort supervision, but a referee decision is final once made and cannot be challenged.

LS-1.3.4

Any offence annuls the hit scored by the fencer at fault if the offence contributed to the scoring of that hit.

LS-1.3.5

Only the Referee may make the final decision on whether a hit occurred. The Referee may not take into account hits delivered before “Play!” or after “Halt!”.

LS-1.3.6

A hit that lands outside the valid target area is not a valid hit.

Longsword rule variants

Longsword tournaments must be organised in exactly one of the following three variants; this must be clearly stated in the event announcement.

  • VOR

  • COMBAT

  • AFTERBLOW

Longsword / VOR (conventional) rules

Validity or priority of hits

Preliminary notes

LS-VOR-1.1.1

Only the Referee decides on the validity or priority of a hit, applying the following fundamental rules which constitute the VOR convention for longsword fencing.

Respect of the fencing phrase

LS-VOR-1.1.2

Every correctly executed attack must be parried or completely avoided, and the fencing phrase must be continuous and coordinated.

LS-VOR-1.1.3

When judging whether an attack is correctly executed, the following must be considered:

LS-VOR-1.1.3.1

A simple attack, direct or indirect, is correctly executed when the extension of the arm and the continuous threatening of the valid target with the point precede the initiation of the lunge or the flèche.

LS-VOR-1.1.3.2

A compound attack is correctly executed when, from the presentation of the first feint with the arm extended, the point threatens the valid target continuously without the attacker withdrawing the arm during the successive movements of the attack and the initiation of the lunge or flèche.

LS-VOR-1.1.3.3

An attack with a step-forward-lunge or a step-forward-flèche is correctly executed when the extension of the arm precedes the completion of the step forward and the initiation of the lunge or flèche.

LS-VOR-1.1.3.4

Simple or compound actions, steps or feints executed with the arm bent are not considered attacks but preparations, exposing the fencer to the initiation of an offensive or offensive–defensive action by the opponent.

When analysing the fencing phrase, to judge priority of the attack the following must be considered

LS-VOR-1.1.2

When analysing the fencing phrase to judge priority of the attack, the following factors must be taken into account:

LS-VOR-1.1.2.1

If the attack is initiated when the opponent is in the “point in line” position (i.e. with the arm extended and the point continually threatening the valid target — longsword: longpoint/langort), the attacker must first deflect the opponent’s weapon. The Referee must ensure that mere blade contact is not considered sufficient to deflect the opponent’s weapon.

LS-VOR-1.1.2.2

If the attempt to deflect the opponent’s blade does not find the blade (dérobement / evasion), the right of attack passes to the opponent.

LS-VOR-1.1.2.3

If the attack is initiated when the opponent is not in point in line, the attack may be executed directly or by disengagement, cut-over, or with feints obliging the opponent to parry.

LS-VOR-1.1.2.4

Continuous forward stepping with the legs crossing constitutes preparation; against such preparation, any simple attack has priority.

LS-VOR-1.1.3

In compound attacks, feints must be executed correctly, i.e.:

LS-VOR-1.1.3.1

A thrust feint must be shown with the arm extended while continuously threatening the valid target with the point;

LS-VOR-1.1.3.2

A cut feint must be shown with the arm extended such that the blade and the arm form an obtuse angle of about 135°, and the cutting edge threatens the valid target;

LS-VOR-1.1.3.3

If during the execution of a compound attack the opponent takes the attacker’s blade during a feint, the opponent has the right to riposte.

LS-VOR-1.1.3.3

In compound attacks the opponent has the right to stop-hit; however, for it to be valid, the stop-hit must precede the conclusion of the attack by one fencing time, i.e. the stop-hit must land before the attacker begins the final movement of their attack.

LS-VOR-1.1.4

Attack by beat or taking of the blade:

LS-VOR-1.1.4.1

An attack by beat or taking of the blade is correctly executed and retains its priority when the beat is made on the foible (the weaker half), i.e. the half of the opponent’s blade farther from the guard.

LS-VOR-1.1.4.2

In an attack by beat or taking of the blade, when the beat is made on the forte (the stronger half), i.e. the half of the opponent’s blade closest to the guard, the attack must be considered incorrectly executed (parried), and this beat gives the opponent the right to an immediate riposte.

LS-VOR-1.1.5

Parry:

LS-VOR-1.1.5.1

A parry (or the complete avoidance of the attack) gives the right to riposte. The simple riposte may be direct or indirect; however, to annul any further actions by the attacker it must be executed immediately, without hesitation or delay.

LS-VOR-1.1.5.2

A parry against thrusts aims to prevent the point from arriving on the target area against which the thrust is directed.

LS-VOR-1.1.5.3

A parry against cuts aims to prevent the hit from arriving on the target area against which the cut is directed.

  • the parry is correctly executed when it prevents the opponent’s hit from arriving before the offensive action is completed, by closing the line in which the attack would be completed;
  • if a parry is correctly executed, the opponent’s attack must be considered parried even if, due to blade flexibility, the point nevertheless reaches the target.

Close quarters

LS-VOR-1.2.1

Priority ends when the strong parts of the weapons meet (including the crossguard), and/or in wrestling actions. If, after contact of the strong parts of the blades, the fencers immediately hit each other, both hits must be annulled. Otherwise, they may separate and continue fencing (under the conventional longsword rules) or transition to wrestling (under the wrestling rules).

Judging hits

The Referee should judge as follows when applying these conventions:

LS-VOR-1.3.2

If within one fencing time only one valid hit occurs, the Referee awards the hit against the fencer who was hit, regardless of its location, force or the manner of execution.

LS-VOR-1.3.3

When during a fencing phrase both fencers land hits simultaneously, this is either a simultaneous action or a double hit.

LS-VOR-1.3.4

A simultaneous action results from the simultaneous decision and execution of an attack by both fencers; in this case, the hits exchanged are annulled for both fencers.

LS-VOR-1.3.5

A double hit, by contrast, results from a faulty action by one of the fencers. Therefore, if there is not one fencing time between the two hits:

LS-VOR-1.3.5.1

Only the fencer who is attacked is counted as hit:

  • if they make a stop-hit into a simple attack;
  • if instead of parrying they attempt to evade but do not succeed;
  • if after a successful parry they pause momentarily, giving the opponent time to renew the attack (redoublement, remise, reprise);
  • if into a compound attack they stop-hit at an incorrect time;
  • if, having point in line (longpoint/langort), their blade is deflected by a beat or taking of the blade, and they then attack or re-establish the line instead of parrying the direct hit.

LS-VOR-1.3.5.2

Only the attacker is counted as hit:

  • if they attack an opponent’s point in line (longpoint/langort) without first deflecting the blade;
  • if they search for the blade but do not find it (opponent evades) and they continue their attack;
  • if during a compound attack the opponent takes the blade, the attacker continues, while the opponent ripostes immediately;
  • if during a compound attack the attacker bends the arm or pauses momentarily, the opponent stop-hits while the attacker continues;
  • if during a compound attack the attacker receives a stop-hit in time (one fencing time before the final movement begins);
  • if their original attack is parried and they score by remise/redoublement/reprise while the opponent’s riposte is immediate, simple, in one fencing time, and without withdrawing the arm.

LS-VOR-1.3.5.3

The Referee must put the fencers back on guard whenever, in case of a double hit, the Referee cannot clearly determine which side committed the fault.

LS-VOR-1.3.6

A hit that occurs beyond one fencing time (a late after-action) is not relevant to the phrase. Such a hit scores no point and does not annul the original hit received.

Longsword / AFTERBLOW

Validity and weighting of hits

LS-AB-1.1.1

Only the Referee decides on hit validity, applying the following fundamental rules.

LS-AB-1.1.1

When judging the correctness of hits, the following must be considered:

  • A hit delivered with a correctly held weapon (two hands) is worth 2 points,
  • A hit delivered with a one-handed weapon grip is worth 1 point.

Judging hits

When applying this longsword rules variant, the Referee must judge as follows:

LS-AB-1.2.1

When, within one fencing time, both fencers receive a hit in a fencing phrase, this may be either a simultaneous hit or a double hit.

LS-AB-1.2.2

Hits must be considered simultaneous when the Referee cannot clearly determine the temporal order of arrival of the two hits.

LS-AB-1.2.3

Hits must be considered double when

  • both hits occur within the same fencing phrase,
  • there is no full fencing-time difference between the two hits, therefore
  • the Referee cannot clearly establish that completion of one hit preceded the start of the movement directly delivering the other hit.
  • The movement directly delivering the hit may be, for example, a simple (direct or indirect) attack/stop-hit/riposte; or, in a compound attack/stop-hit/riposte, the final motion aimed at the final target.
  • Examples (examining action timing, not action priority): stop-hit into a simple attack, or into the final movement of a compound attack, where both actions land.

LS-AB-1.2.5

After-hits

LS-AB-1.2.5.1

A hit is considered an after-hit and reduces the value (weight) of the original hit if it is executed as follows:

  • after a fencer has received a valid hit,
  • the fencer lands a hit with an immediate, simple, after-action executed without indecision or delay;
  • without a clearly perceptible break/separation in the fencing, or a re-evaluation of fencing roles.
  • Examples (examining action timing, not action priority):
    • a stop-hit lands during a feinted attack, before the final movement of the attack has begun, but the attacker finishes the attack (the attack lands outside fencing time and therefore qualifies as an after-hit);
    • an after-hit landed with a simple riposte after a failed parry (received hit)

LS-AB-1.2.5.2

For consistent rule application, the head Referee may determine a clearly perceptible interruption of the fencing phrase based on the following observable events:

  • When the Referee perceives the first hit, the bout is stopped; actions initiated after the halt must be annulled, and these belong to first-group disciplinary offences (cf. General / Conduct of the bout).
  • A clearly perceptible temporal difference exists if, between the two hits, any of the following is observed:
    • clear withdrawal/raising-back of the weapon, or withdrawal of threat
    • initiation of the next step instead of/before the after-cut or after-thrust
    • a moment when the opponent is no longer under immediate threat

LS-AB-1.2.6

In cases of simultaneous hits AND double hits, both fencers are considered hit. Hits must be awarded as follows:

  • if both fencers landed with a two-handed grip, 1 point must be awarded against both fencers
  • if both fencers landed with a one-handed grip, 1 point must be awarded against both fencers
  • if one fencer landed one-handed and the other two-handed simultaneously, 1 point must be awarded against the fencer who held the weapon one-handed.

LS-AB-1.2.7

In case of after-hits, the hit must be awarded against the fencer who was hit first in temporal order. The after-hit is not awarded in its own right, but only from the perspective of whether it qualifies as a valid after-hit relative to the first, original hit.

LS-AB-1.2.9

An after-hit (regardless of whether executed with one or two hands on the weapon) reduces the number of points awardable relative to the original hit:

  • if the original hit is worth 2 points, the after-hit reduces the registered score to 1
  • if the original hit is worth 1 point, the after-hit reduces the registered score to 0.

LS-AB-1.2.10

Defence against after-actions

LS-AB-1.2.10.1

If the fencer who delivered the original hit defends with the blade against the actually executed after-action (the fact of the defence is sufficient; a riposte is not required), the registered score is increased:

  • if the original hit is worth 2 points, defending the after-action increases the registered score to 3
  • if the original hit is worth 1 point, defending the after-action increases the registered score to 2

LS-AB-1.2.10.2

An after-action started before the halt command may be defended, but any further action initiation after “Halt!”, including a riposte from defending the after-action, still belongs to first-group disciplinary offences.

LS-AB-1.2.10.3

Preventing/deflecting hits within one fencing time (e.g. closing cuts/thrusts) is not considered defence against an after-action.

LS-AB-1.2.10.4

Defence against an after-action may be awarded only if it is executed after a valid original hit, against an actual valid after-action, with an actual defensive action: i.e. a new, immediate, actual parry movement executed after receiving/landing the original hit (cf. above: After-hits).

LS-AB-1.2.10.5

The failure or invalidity of an attempted after-action (e.g. too short, misses, falls onto the opponent’s sword) is NOT in itself considered defence against an after-action.

LS-AB-1.2.10.6

If no actual after-action was executed, defence against an after-action cannot be awarded, not even if

  • the fencer who landed the original hit creates blade contact through attack reprise or blade attack.
  • the opponent, after being hit, initiates an action that does not qualify as an after-action (delay, interrupted fencing phrase, action initiated after halt).
  • Cf. after-hits and their conditions LS-AB-1.2.5.

LS-AB-1.2.11

If a simultaneous or double hit is followed by an after-hit within the same fencing phrase, the after-hit must be ignored.

LS-AB-1.2.12

If there is a double hit or hit-after-hit where one is valid and the other invalid (off-target, delivered after leaving the piste, etc.), only the valid hit must be awarded, as if it were the original and only hit. If an additional after-hit then occurs (e.g. a reprise after an off-target hit), it must be ignored.

LS-AB-1.2.13

If the Referee cannot judge whether an alleged hit occurred or is valid, the hit or double hit is annulled, no point is awarded, and the fencers are reset where the bout was stopped (cf.: 03-general / Ground won or lost).

LS-AB-1.2.11

If the original hit is invalid (off-target, or delivered after leaving the piste, etc.), the subsequent after-hit is not a scoring action, must be annulled, and the fencers must be reset on guard to the on-guard lines.

Disciplinary Rules for Competitions

Scope

Personal scope of the rules

Maintaining order and discipline

DIS-1.2.1

Fencers must precisely and honestly comply with the MHS competition rules and statutes, any special rules applicable to the given event, the traditional customs of courtesy and propriety, and the instructions of officials.

DIS-1.2.2

They expressly submit themselves to the following provisions based on the principles of order, discipline and sportsmanship. In case of breach, depending on the facts and circumstances, the competent disciplinary authority may apply the prescribed sanctions, with or without a prior warning.

DIS-1.2.3

All persons participating in or present at a fencing competition must respect the MHS Statutes. Everyone must respect order and no one may disrupt the smooth running of the competition. During bouts, no one is entitled to approach the arena, give advice to the fencers, criticise or insult the referee or assistant referee, or attempt to influence them in any way. Even the team captain must remain in the designated place and may intervene only in the cases and manner described in DIS-1.3.14. The Referee must immediately stop any conduct that disturbs the smooth conduct of the bout (see DIS-2.1.2–DIS-2.1.4). Anyone who threatens or insults an official for any reason commits a 4th-group offence and must be sanctioned in accordance with DIS-4.3.15–DIS-4.3.16.

DIS-1.2.4

Any person who insults or threatens an official for any reason may be immediately disqualified and/or expelled from the premises.

DIS-1.2.4

The Referee and/or the Organising Team may, within their own authority, decide to expel from the competition area any person whose gestures, behaviour or language disrupt the orderly running of the competition.

The competitors

Honour commitment

DIS-1.3.1

By the mere fact of their participation, fencers pledge on their honour that they will comply with the rules; submit to the decisions and instructions of officials; treat the Referees (referees and assistant referees) with respect; and conscientiously follow their instructions and decisions.

Refusal to fence an opponent

DIS-1.3.2

A fencer may not take part in the competition if they refuse to fence another competitor who is properly entered for the event. Breach of this rule must be sanctioned as set out in the 4th group of disciplinary offences.

Timely appearance

DIS-1.3.3

Fencers must appear at the specified place and time for their pool round, bout or direct elimination bout, and at the designated equipment-check time before their bout, fully equipped in conformity with the rules and ready to fence, and whenever the Referee calls them to do so during the competition.

DIS-1.3.4

When presenting themselves to start a bout, fencers must enter the arena fully ready to fence — in regulation clothing, jacket closed, glove on, and weapon in hand.

DIS-1.3.5

If during the competition a fencer does not appear in the arena when called by the Referee:

  • The absent fencer receives a yellow card;
  • One minute after the first call, they are called a second time; if still absent, the fencer receives a red card;
  • One minute after the second call, they receive a third and final call; continued absence results in exclusion from the event.

Fencer etiquette

DIS-1.3.6

DIS-1.3.6.1

Competitors must fence honestly and in strict compliance with this ruleset. Any breach entails the sanctions recorded here.

DIS-1.3.6.2

Every bout must remain courteous and honest. Any irregular action (a flèche that ends by pushing the opponent, confused/disorderly fencing, irregular movements, violent hits, punches, kicks, hitting with a basket/crossguard, deliberately falling to avoid being hit) or unsportsmanlike behaviour is expressly forbidden — see also DIS-4.1.1–DIS-4.1.5, DIS-4.3.20. If such an offence arises, any hit scored by the fencer at fault must be annulled.

DIS-1.3.7

Before the start of a bout, the two fencers salute (fencing salute) their opponent, the Referee and the audience. After the last hit is delivered they must wait calmly for the Referee’s decision on the on-guard line. Then they must perform the fencing salute, greeting the opponent, the Referee and the audience. The bout ends thereafter. If one or both fencers refuse this, the Referee applies the sanction corresponding to 4th-group offences against the offender(s).

DIS-1.3.8

During or after the bout, even after leaving the arena, any unsportsmanlike behaviour is forbidden, such as violently or dangerously throwing the mask or other equipment, and must be sanctioned as a 4th-group offence.

Personal attitude

DIS-1.3.12

Fencers must fence sportsmanlike until the end of the competition, to the best of their ability, to achieve the best possible placing, without gifting hits to anyone or accepting gifted hits from anyone. Breach of the rule must be sanctioned as a 4th-group offence.

DIS-1.3.14

The team captain:
In team competitions only the team captain may approach the Referee to clarify technical questions or to submit a complaint. The procedure for complaints is governed by DIS-5.2.2–DIS-5.2.5. Team members who precisely followed the team captain’s instructions cannot be held responsible by other competent bodies; however, they are personally responsible for any acts not ordered by the captain and for any offences they commit that breach this ruleset.

Coaches and accompanying staff

Audience

Disciplinary authorities and their powers

Competent bodies and persons

The Referee

DIS-2.1.1

The Referee not only directs the bout, judges hits and checks equipment, but is also responsible for maintaining order in the bouts they supervise.

DIS-2.1.3

When directing bouts, judging hits and checking equipment, the Referee may — taking circumstances into account, with or without prior warning — penalise fencers for offences by annulling a hit actually scored, awarding a penalty hit against a fencer even though no hit actually occurred, or excluding the competitor from the given bout/event. Decisions containing findings of fact may not be altered.

DIS-2.1.4

The Referee’s authority extends to all fencers participating in or contributing to the competition. The Referee may propose to the Organising Team to expel anyone from the venue, including spectators, coaches or other attendants.

DIS-2.1.5

The Referee may propose to the Organising Team further sanctions they consider appropriate (exclusion from the whole competition, suspension or disqualification) (see DIS-2.1.7.3).

DIS-2.1.6

The appeal body regarding the Referee's decisions is the delegate of the Referees' Committee, or the MHS inspector (if there is no delegate).

The Organising Team / Szervező Csapat at official MHS competitions

DIS-2.1.7 The Organising Team / Szervező Team at official MHS competitions. DIS-2.1.7.1

The Organising Team, the delegates of the Referees' Committee and the MHS inspector have authority over every competitor who participates in or is present at the fencing competition they supervise.
DIS-2.1.7.2

If necessary, they may intervene in any dispute on their own initiative.
DIS-2.1.7.3

They must maintain order and discipline during the competition and may apply the sanctions prescribed in this ruleset.
DIS-2.1.7.4

The Organising Team must forward the disciplinary sanctions imposed during the competition to the MHS central office, as well as any requests for reprimand, suspension, permanent suspension, extension of sanctions, or final appeals.
DIS-2.1.7.5

The Organising Team is responsible for implementing imposed sanctions where no appeal is possible or where the appeal has no suspensive effect.

DIS-2.1.8

Against a spontaneous decision of the Organising Team / delegate / inspector, or a decision issued by them in first instance, an appeal may be filed with the MHS Disciplinary Committee.

DIS-2.1.9

Every decision of the Organising Team / delegate / inspector is immediately enforceable. During the competition, no appeal has suspensive effect on execution.

Sanctions

Classification of sanctions

DIS-3.1.1

Different offences must be sanctioned by different types of penalties.

DIS-3.1.1.1

Bout-related penalties, applicable to offences committed during fencing:

  • loss of ground
  • annulling a hit actually scored
  • awarding a penalty hit (a hit not actually received)
  • exclusion from the event

DIS-3.1.1.2

Disciplinary penalties, applicable to offences against order, discipline and sporting spirit:

  • awarding a penalty hit (a hit not actually received)
  • exclusion from the event
  • exclusion from the whole tournament
  • expulsion from the venue
  • temporary exclusion from events organised by the Federation or the organiser

DIS-3.1.2

All listed penalties — except permanent suspension — may be imposed at the competition by the competent authorities: the Referee and the Organising Team.

Bout-related penalties

Annulling a hit actually scored

DIS-3.2.1

A hit on valid target may be annulled if it did not occur during effective fighting time; if the fencer stepped out; because of electrical equipment failure; if violence occurred while delivering the hit; or for any other reason recorded in the rules (in line with the technical rules).

Awarding a penalty hit (a hit not actually received)

DIS-3.2.2

A fencer may be penalised by a hit even though no hit was actually received, if the fencer crosses the rear boundary with both feet, or if they hinder their opponent in an impermissible way (a flèche with collision, initiating gripping/wrestling when not permitted, etc.).

Exclusion

DIS-3.2.3

A fencer may be excluded from the event if they carry out a grossly violent or vindictive action, if they do not fence to the best of their ability, or if they profit from a fraudulent agreement with an opponent.

DIS-3.2.4

A competitor excluded from the event may not continue fencing even if they already advanced to the next round. They lose their placing in the individual event and all fencers placed below move up one place. Where necessary, the two third places must be determined based on the ranking number used to build the tableau. In every case, only fencers who scored points in the competition move up.

Disciplinary penalties

Exclusion from the event

DIS-3.3.1

A fencer may be excluded from the event for disciplinary reasons as well (not appearing properly on the piste; weapons not regulation; improper behaviour towards an official, etc.). The consequences set out in DIS-3.2.4 apply accordingly.

Expulsion from the venue; exclusion from the tournament

DIS-3.3.2

A competitor excluded from the whole tournament may no longer take part in any event at that competition, neither in the same nor in another weapon.

DIS-3.3.3

If exclusion applies to an entire team, each team member’s case must be examined separately and their sanctions may differ depending on circumstances.

DIS-3.3.4

Any participant or non-fencing attendant present at the competition (coach, technician, supporter, official, spectator, etc.) may be expelled. Expulsion means the person may not remain at the venue for the duration of the competition or the given event. This measure is not appealable under any circumstances.

Disqualification

DIS-3.3.5

Disqualification in good faith does not necessarily entail a fixed-term or permanent suspension; in case of fraudulent intent, further sanctions may be requested.

DIS-3.3.6

A team that fields a competitor who has been disqualified is itself subject to the same fate and is disqualified.

DIS-3.3.7

The consequences described for exclusion apply appropriately to disqualification as well (see DIS-3.2.3–DIS-3.2.4).

Reprimand

DIS-3.3.8

Where imposing a more severe penalty is not justified, the fencer or official must be reprimanded.

Fixed-term suspension

DIS-3.3.9

A suspended competitor may not participate in official MHS competitions for the duration of the suspension.

DIS-3.3.10

Other (non-competitor) suspended persons may not practise their function/profession during the territorial scope and duration of the suspension.

Permanent suspension

DIS-3.3.11

The consequences of permanent suspension are the same as for fixed-term suspension, but last indefinitely.

Publication of sanctions

DIS-3.4.1

The Organising Team must immediately inform the MHS Office about sanctions imposed during competitions and the reasons for imposing them.

SANCTIONS AND THE BODIES ENTITLED TO IMPOSE THEM

Types (groups) of penalties

DIS-4.1.1

Three types of penalties may be applied in the cases listed in the table in DIS-4.3.20. If the Referee penalises a fencer who committed several offences at the same time, the penalty for the less serious fault must be imposed first.

DIS-4.1.2

Penalties accumulate and apply within a bout, except the BLACK CARD, which entails exclusion from the event and suspension from the remainder of the tournament.

DIS-4.1.3

However, if a team is excluded from a competition because one of its members received a black card, the team is not excluded from future competitions. Only the penalised fencer is suspended in accordance with DIS-4.1.2, and during the suspension they may not be a member of any team.

DIS-4.1.4

Certain offences entail annulling any hit scored by the competitor at fault. During a bout, only those hits affected by the offence are to be annulled.

DIS-4.1.5

The penalties are as follows:

DIS-4.1.5.1

Warning, expressed by the Referee showing a YELLOW CARD and indicating the fencer at fault. The fencer at fault acknowledges that any further offence on their part will entail a penalty hit.

DIS-4.1.5.2

Penalty hit, expressed by the Referee showing a RED CARD and indicating the fencer at fault. In that case, one hit is added to the opponent’s score, which — if it is the final hit — may lead to loss of the bout. Furthermore, every RED CARD can be followed only by another RED CARD or a BLACK CARD, depending on the nature of the subsequent offence.

DIS-4.1.5.3

Exclusion from the event and suspension from the remainder of the tournament, expressed by the Referee showing a BLACK CARD and indicating the fencer at fault.

DIS-4.1.5.4

Expulsion from the venue (applicable against any person disturbing the order of the competition).

DIS-4.1.6

All warnings (yellow cards), penalty hits (red cards) and exclusions (black cards), and the group to which they belong, must be recorded in the bout/pool/team match report.

DIS-4.1.7

All warnings (YELLOW CARD), penalty hits (RED CARD) and exclusions (BLACK CARD) must be recorded on the score sheet, together with the disciplinary group to which they belong.

Authority

DIS-4.1.8

A summary of offences and penalties found in different parts of the competition rules is contained in the table. These are divided into four groups. Every penalty is within the Referee’s authority; however, the Organising Team reserves the right to intervene on its own initiative.

First-group offences

DIS-4.1.9

In the first group, the first offence entails a YELLOW CARD (warning). If during the same bout the fencer repeatedly commits the same or another offence in this group, the Referee penalises each time with a RED CARD (penalty hit). If the fencer at fault has already received a RED CARD in that bout due to an offence listed in the Second or Third Group, then even the first offence in the First Group results in a further RED CARD.

DIS-4.3.10

In team matches, counting of first-group offences restarts at the beginning of each relay/bout (in each relay the first offence results in a YELLOW CARD), except for team-wide warnings indicated in the table, after which any First Group offence committed by any team member for the remainder of the match must be penalised by a RED CARD.

Second-group offences

DIS-4.3.11

All second-group offences must be penalised by a RED CARD (penalty hit) from the first offence onwards.

Third-group offences

DIS-4.3.12

The first third-group offence must be penalised by a RED CARD (penalty hit), even if the fencer at fault has previously received a RED CARD for an offence in the First or Second Group.

DIS-4.3.13

If during the same bout the fencer repeatedly commits the same or another third-group offence, the sanction is a BLACK CARD (exclusion from the event; suspension from the remainder of the tournament).

DIS-4.3.14

In case of disturbance by a person not on the piste/arena:

  • On the first occasion, a YELLOW CARD warning is imposed, valid for the whole competition. This must be recorded on the bout report and recorded by the Organising Team.
  • On the second occasion during the competition, the sanction is a BLACK CARD.
  • In particularly serious cases (whether on or off the piste), the Referee may immediately exclude/expel the offender.

Fourth-group offences

DIS-4.3.15

Commission of a fourth-group offence must be penalised immediately by a BLACK CARD (exclusion from the event; suspension from the remainder of the tournament).

DIS-4.3.16

Furthermore, in MHS competitions (and in any competition organised by a confederation that has submitted itself to the MHS disciplinary code), every black card must be reported to the President of MHS within 10 days. The President evaluates whether the seriousness of the offence justifies forwarding the inspector’s or Organising Team’s report to the chair of the Legal Committee, requesting the establishment of a Disciplinary Tribunal to determine whether further sanctions are necessary beyond the sanction imposed at the competition.

Annulling a hit because of a rule violation

DIS-4.3.17

A hit must be annulled if the Referee determines that it was achieved by means of a rule violation that had a direct causal connection to the fencing action that led to the hit.

DIS-4.3.18

A rule violation is considered directly and causally connected if, in the Referee’s judgement, the hit could not have occurred in the same way or at the same moment without committing the rule violation.

DIS-4.3.19

A hit must not be annulled merely because a rule violation occurred, if:

  • the rule violation did not directly take part in executing the scoring action (roles/initiative were re-evaluated between the violation and the hit);
  • the rule violation was not connected to the tactical or physical conditions that enabled the hit.

DIS-4.3.20

Table of offences and penalties

The table is intended as a convenient summary; it does not replace the text of the relevant provisions, which are authoritative in case of doubt.
